title: Question 2
text: Let \(A\) be a ring and let \(A[x]\) be the ring of polynomials in an indeterminate \(x\), with coefficients in \(A\). Let \(f=a_0+a_1x+\cdots+a_nx^n\in A[x]\).

objectID: books/Atiyah McDonald Commutative Algebra/1. Rings and Ideals/Exercises/2/2.html#section
href: books/Atiyah McDonald Commutative Algebra/1. Rings and Ideals/Exercises/2/2.html#section
title: Question 2
text:
(i). Prove that \(f\) is a unit in \(A[x]\) \(\Leftrightarrow\) \(a_0\) is an unit in \(A\) and \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\) are nilpotent.
Hint: If \(b_0+\cdots b_mx^m\) is the inverse of \(f\), prove by induction on \(r\), that \(a_n^{r+1}b_{m-r}=0\). Hence show that \(a_n\) is nilpotent and then use Ex. \(1\).

objectID: books/Atiyah McDonald Commutative Algebra/1. Rings and Ideals/Exercises/2/2.html#section-1
href: books/Atiyah McDonald Commutative Algebra/1. Rings and Ideals/Exercises/2/2.html#section-1
title: Question 2
text:
Solution:
Suppose \(g=b_0+\cdots +b_mx^m\). Let \(h=fg\). If \(h = \sum_i h_ix^i\). Then \(h_i=0\) for \(i>n+m\), and \[h_i = \sum_{k=0}^ia_{i-k}\,b_k,\quad 0\leq i\leq n+m\]
Interlude: A couple of points about polynomials
One of the two fundamental properties of polynomials is that every polynomial has a unique decomposition as a sum of monomials. Monomials are special polynomials that have a non zero component in only one degree. The \(0\) polynomial, is the polynomial whose coefficient in every degree is \(0\). In particular \(0=0 + 0\cdot x+0\cdot x^2+\cdots 0\cdot x^n + \cdots\). The uniquness of the decomposition of a polynomial in terms of monomials implies that this is the unique decomposition for the \(0\) polynomial. This means that if a polynomial is the \(0\) polynomial, then its component in every degree is \(0\). If \(a(x)\) and \(b(x)\) are two polynomials such that \(a(x)=b(x)\) or equivalently \(a(x)-b(x)=0\), then \(a(x)-b(x) = \sum_i(a_i-b_i)x^i = 0\). So \(a_i-b_i=0\) for all \(i\) or \(a_i=b_i\) for all \(i\). So two polynomials are equal only if their component in each degree are equal. This stems from the unique decomposition of polynomial as a sum of monomials.
By the way for a polynomial \(a(x)=\sum_ia_ix^i\). We call \(a_kx^k\), the component of \(a(x)\) in degree \(k\), while we call \(a_k\) the coefficient of \(a(x)\) in degree \(k\).
The second fundamental property of the polynomials is how they multiply, \(ax^n \cdot bx^m = abx^{m+n}\). Using this and the distributive and commutative properties of the operations in commutative rings we get the multiplication for general polynomials.
Suppose \(g\) is the (multiplicative)inverse of \(f\). \[(b_0+\cdots +b_mx^m)(a_0+a_1x+\cdots+a_nx^n) = 1.\]
So \(h=fg = 1\). Then \(h_0=1\) and \(h_i=0\) for all \(i>0\).
\(h_0 = \sum_{k=0}^0a_{0-k}b_k = a_0b_0\), as the sum has only one summand. So \(a_0b_0=1\). This implies that \(f_0 = a_0\) is a unit.
Now we want to prove by induction that \(a_n^{r+1}b_{m-r}=0\) for \(0\leq r\leq m\). This will imply that \(a_n^{m+1}b_0=0\). But \(b_0\) is a unit as we just proved. This will imply that \(a_n^{m+1}=0\). This will imply that \(a_n\) is nilpotent. Hence \(a_nx^n\) is nilpotent. But by Ex \(1\), \(f^{(n-1)}(x) = f(x)-a_nx^n\) is a unit, where \(f^{(n-1)}(x) = a_0+\cdots+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}\) is the polynomial got from \(f(x)\) by keeping terms upto degree \(n-1\). If \(n-1>0\), then we can repeat this process to show that \(a_{n-1}\) is nilpotent. Iterating this \(n-2\) more times we can show that \(a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_{n-2}\) are nilpotent. Hence we have proved that if \(f(x)\) is an unit then \(a_0\) is an unit and \(a_i\) is nilpotent for \(i>0\).
If \(n+m=0\), then \(f\) is a degree \(0\) polynomial and a unit. So its coefficient in all positive degree is \(0\), so it satisfies the assertion. If \(n+m>0\), then \(h_{n+m} = \sum_{k=0}^{n+m}a_{n+m-k}b_k = a_nb_m\), as this sum also has only one summand. So \(a_nb_m=0\). So \(a_n^{0+1}b_{m-0} =0\). Thus the statement “\(a_n^{r+1}b_{m-r}=0\)” is true for \(r=0\).
Let us make the induction hypothesis that for \(1 < r < k\leq m\), \(a_n^{r+1}b_{m-r}=0\).
\(h_{n+m-k} = a_{n+m-k}b_0+a_{n+m-k-1}b_1+\cdots+a_0b_{n+m-k} = 0\). As \(k\leq m\), we have \(n+m-k\geq n>0\). So \(h_{n+m-k}=0\). Also note \(a_{n+(m-k)}=a_{n+(m-k)-1}=\cdots=a_{n+1}=0\). So we have \(h_{n+m-k} = a_nb_{m-k}+a_{n-1}b_{(m-k)+1}+\cdots+a_0b_{n+m-k} = 0\). Let us multiply by \(a_n^{k}\), we get \(a_n^k(a_nb_{m-k}+a_{n-1}b_{(m-k)+1}+\cdots+a_0b_{n+m-k}) = 0 = a_n^k\cdot 0 = 0\). So \(a_n^{k+1}b_{m-k}+a_{n-1}a_n^kb_{m-(k-1)}+\cdots+a_0a_n^{n-1}a_n^{k-n+1}b_{m-(k-n)}=0\). But by induction hypothesis \(a_n^kb_{m-(k-1)},a_n^{k-1}b_{m-(k-2)},\ldots, a_nb_m\) are \(0\). Also if \(k-n<0\), then \(b_{m+1},\ldots,b_{m-(k-n)}\) are also \(0\). So \(a_{n-1}a_n^kb_{m-(k-1)}+\cdots+a_0a_n^{n-1}a_n^{k-n+1}b_{m-(k-n)}=0\). Hence \(a_n^{k+1}b_{m-k}=0\). So the induction step holds good. So \(a_n^{r+1}b_{m-r}=0\) holds for \(1\leq r\leq m\).
For the reverse implication note that if \(a_i\) is nilpotent for \(i>0\), then \(a_ix^i\) is also nilpotent. The sum of two nilpotent elements \(a,b\) is also nilpotent. Suppose \(a^m=b^n=0\), then \((a+b)^{m+n-1} = \sum \binom{m+n-1}{p}a^pb^{m+n-1-p}\). But for \(0\leq p\leq m+n-1\) either \(p\geq m\) (and)or \(m+n-1-p\geq n\). So the product in each of the summands in this sum is \(0\). So \((a+b)^{m+n-1}=0\). So \(a+b\) is also nilpotent. From this we can conclude that a finite sum of nilpotent elements is nilpotent. Hence the sum \(\sum_{i>0}a_ix^i\) is nilpotent. Since \(a_0\) is an unit. Using exercise \(1\) the sum \(\sum_{i\geq 0}a_ix^i\) is an unit. Note that there are only finitely many terms in these sums.
Note: If a polynomial \(f(x)\) is a unit, then \(f_0\) is a unit. This also holds good for polynomials in more than \(1\) variable and also in power series rings in one or more than one variable. The proof of this fact in these rings is similar to the proof for polynomials in \(1\) variable case.

text: (ii). \(f\) is nilpotent \(\Leftrightarrow\) \(a_0,a_1,\ldots,a_n\) are nilpotent.

objectID: books/Atiyah McDonald Commutative Algebra/1. Rings and Ideals/Exercises/2/2.html#section-3
href: books/Atiyah McDonald Commutative Algebra/1. Rings and Ideals/Exercises/2/2.html#section-3
title: Question 2
text:
Solution:
As in the proof of the reverse implication in part (i). if \(a_i,i\geq 0\) are nilpotent then \(a_ix^i\) are nilpotent. Hence the sum \(\sum_{i\geq 0}a_ix^i\) is nilpotent. So \(f(x)\) is nilpotent.
Note that we cannot have that \(a, a+b\) are nilpotent but \(b\) is not nilpotent for elements \(a,b\). It is so because \(b = (a+b)-(a)\) and the sum and difference of two nilpotents is nilpotent. But the sum of two non nilpotents can be nilpotent. For example \(1+(-1)=0\).
The constant term of \(f^r\) is \(a_0^r\). So if \(f^R=0\). We must also have that the constant term of \(f^R=0\). So we have that \(a_0^R=0\). Hence \(a_0\) is nilpotent. A similar argument will imply the leading coefficient \(a_n\) must also be nilpotent. Specifically if \(f^R=0\). Then the coefficient of \(x^{nR}\) in \(f^R\) is \(a_n^R\). Hence \(a_n^R=0\). Hence \(a_n\) is nilpotent. Thus \(a_nx^n\) is nilpotent. So \(f-a_nx^n = a_0+\cdots+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}\) is also nilpotent. Iterating this \(n-1\) times we will get that \(a_0,a_1,\ldots,a_{n-1}\) are nilpotent.

title: Question 2
text: (iii). \(f\) is a zero-divisor \(\Leftrightarrow\) there exists \(a\neq 0\) in \(A\) such that \(af=0\).[Choose a \(^{\text{nonzero}}\) polynomial \(g=b_0+b_1x+\cdots+b_mx^m\) of least degree \(m\) such that \(fg=0\). Then \(a_nb_m=0\), hence \(a_ng=0\) (because \(a_ng\) annihilates \(f\) and has degree \(< m\)). Now show by induction that \(a_{n-r}g=0\,(0\leq r\leq n)\).]

objectID: books/Atiyah McDonald Commutative Algebra/1. Rings and Ideals/Exercises/2/2.html#section-5
href: books/Atiyah McDonald Commutative Algebra/1. Rings and Ideals/Exercises/2/2.html#section-5
title: Question 2
text:
Solution:
Given an element \(m\) of a module \(M\) over a ring \(R\), consider the map \[R\to M,\quad r\mapsto rm.\] The image of this map is commonly denoted as \(\langle m\rangle\) or \(Rm\) is called the cyclic submodule generated by \(m\) in \(M\). The kernel of this map is the set of elements \(\{r\in R: rm=0\}\). This kernel is called the Annhilator of \(m\), and is denoted \(\text{Ann}_R\,m\). If one things of multiplication by elements of a ring as an action of the ring on the module(\(\phi_r(m)=rm\)), then elements in \(\ann{m}\) kill or annhilate \(m\) under this action.
Clearly \(f\) is a zero-divisor if and only it has non zero Annihilator.
This exercise asks us to prove that if the Annhilator of a polynomial is nonzero then the Annhilator contains a degree \(0\) element.
When we are considering the Annhilator of an element \(r\) of a ring, we are considering \(R\) as a module over itself.
Suppose \(f\) is a zero divisor. Equivalently \(\text{Ann}_R\,f \neq 0\). If a subset of the polynomial ring contains nonzero elements, then the set of degrees of the nonzero elements in that subset has a least degree. As the Annhilator \(\ann{f}\) is nonzero then there is a least degree among the degrees of the nonzero polynomials in it. Let \(g = \sum_{r=0}^mb_rx^r\) be an element of \(\ann{r}\) of least degree.
If \(\deg g =0\), then then \(f\) satisfies the condition, that we needed to prove.
Suppose \(\deg g > 0\). We have \(gf=0\). So \((gf)_{n+m}=b_ma_n=0\). Note \(ga_n\in\ann{r}\). Also \(\deg a_ng < m = \deg g\) as the coefficient of \(x^m\) in \(a_ng\) which is \(a_nb_m\) is \(0\). So \(a_ng\) can not be nonzero, as it contradicts that \(m=\deg g\) is the least among the degrees of non zero elements in the annhilator \(\ann{f}\).
So \(a_ng = 0\). This is equivalent to saying \(a_nb_r=0\) for \(r=0,1,\ldots,m\). In other words \(a_n\in\ann{\{b_r:0\leq r\leq m\}}\).
If we prove that \(a_i\in \ann{\{b_r:0\leq r\leq m\}}\) for \(i=0,\ldots,n\). This will imply that \(b_r\in\ann{\{a_i:0\leq i\leq n\}}\) for all \(r\). This will imply that \(b_r\in\ann{f}\). Since \(g\neq 0\), atleast one \(b_r\neq 0\). So there exists a non zero degree 0 element in \(\ann{f}\). This will be the solution to the given question.
We will now prove that \(a_i\in \ann{\{b_r:0\leq r\leq m\}}\) for \(i=0,\ldots,n\). We will use induction to prove this. Note that we have assumed \(m>0\) or that \(\deg g>0\).
We have proved this statement for \(i=n\). This is the initial case. We need to prove this for \(i=0,1,\ldots,n\). The induction hypothesis is: Suppose this statement is true for \(i>k\), where \(k=0,\ldots,n-1\). The induction step is to prove this for \(i=k\), under the induction hypthesis. So we need to prove \(a_k\in\ann{\{b_r:0\leq r\leq m\}}\). This is equivalent to proving \(a_kg=0\).
By the fundamental property of \(g\), \(gf=0\). \(f=f_1+f_2\), where \(f_1 = \sum_{i=0}^k a_ix^i\), and \(f_2 = \sum_{i>k} a_ix^i\). By the induction hypothesis \(a_ig=0\) for \(i>k\). This implies that \(f_2g=0\). So \(f_1g=fg-f_2g=0\). So \(g\) annhilates \(f_1\). The coefficient of \(x^{k+m}\) in \(f_1g\) is \(a_kb_m\) and it should also be \(0\). So \(a_kb_m=0\). This implies that: \(\deg a_kg<m\). Since \(a_kg\in\ann{f}\) this implies that \(a_kg=0\). This proves the induction step.
We have used crucially if \(r\in R\) annhilates the leading coefficient of \(g\), then it must annhilate \(g\).
This concludes the proof.

title: Question 2
text: (iv). \(f\) is said to be primitive if \((a_0,a_1,\ldots,a_n)=(1)\). Prove that if \(f,g\in A[x]\), then \(fg\) is primitive \(\Leftrightarrow\) \(f\) and \(g\) are primitive.

objectID: books/Atiyah McDonald Commutative Algebra/1. Rings and Ideals/Exercises/2/2.html#section-7
href: books/Atiyah McDonald Commutative Algebra/1. Rings and Ideals/Exercises/2/2.html#section-7
title: Question 2
text:
Solution:
The notation \((a_0,a_1,\ldots,a_n)\) denotes the ideal generated by the elements \(a_0,a_1,\ldots,a_n\). If \(a\in (b)\), for \(a,b\) in a ring \(R\), then \(a=br\) for some \(r\in R\). Hence when \(a\in (b)\), we sometimes say \(b\) divides \(a\) or \(b|a\). If \(a\in (b)\) and \(b\in (a)\), then \(a=rb\) and \(b=r'a\) for some \(r,r'\) in the ring. So \(a=rr'a\) and \(b=r'rb\). This implies \((1-rr')a=0\) and \((1-r'r)b=0\). If \(R\) is an integral domain and \(a,b\) are nonzero elements, then we must have \(1-r'r=0\) or \(r'r=1\). Hence when \(R\) is an integral domain and \(a,b\) are two nonzero elements dividing each other then \(a=rb\) and \(b=r'a\), where \(r,r'\) are units. We also have that \((a)=(b)\). Sometimes they are called associates. The terms like divisibility are mostly used in integral domains. In integral domains \((a)=(b)\Leftrightarrow a|b \text{ and } b|a\). In this context if \((a_0,a_1,\ldots,a_n)\) is a principal ideal, say it is \((r)\), then \(r\) is said to be the gcd of \(a_0,a_1,\ldots,a_n\). \((1)=R\), and if for two elements \((a,b)=(1)=R\), we say \(a,b\) are coprime. \((1)\) is called the unit ideal(the ideal generated by any unit).
For this question our base ring is \(A\), rather than our usual \(R\).
A polynomial \(f(x)=\sum_{i=0}^na_ix^i\) is primitive if \((a_0,a_1,\ldots,a_n)=(1)=A\). If \(f(x)\) is not primitive then \((a_0,a_1,\ldots,a_n)\neq A\). But it need not be a principal ideal, that is if \(f\) is not primitive it does not mean that \((a_0,a_1,\ldots,a_n)=(a)\) for some \(a\in A\). This ideal may not be principal in general. Ofcourse if \(A\) is a Principal Ideal Domain then this ideal is principal, and in this case \((a_0,a_1,\ldots,a_n)=(c_f)\), the generator \(c_f\) is called the content of \(f\).
Given a polynomial \(p_0+p_1x+\cdots +p^kx^k\), let \(c(p)\) denote the ideal generated by the coefficients of \(p\). So \(c(p)=\langle p_0,p_1,\ldots,p_k\rangle\). \(c(p)\) is called the content ideal of the polynomial \(p\).
Let \(f=\sum_{i=0}^na_i\,x^i\) and let \(g=\sum_{j=0}^mb_j\,x^j\). So \(c(f)\) and \(c(g)\) are the ideals \((a_0,a_1,\ldots,a_n)\), and \((b_0,b_1,\ldots,b_m)\) respectively. Then the product ideal \(c(f)Cg\) is generated by \(\{a_ib_j:0\leq i\leq n,0\leq j\leq m\}\). Each coefficient of the product polynomial \(fg\) is a sum of some products \(a_ib_j\). Hence each coefficient of \(fg\) is in the ideal \(c(f)c(g)\). So the ideal \(C_{fg}\) is a subideal of \(c(f)c(g)\). That is \(C_{fg}\subset c(f)c(g)\). We have the following sequence of inclusions of ideals \[C_{fg}\subset c(f)c(g)\subset c(f)\cap c(g).\]
If \(C_{fg}=A\). Then \(c(f)\cap c(g)=A\). As \(c(f)\cap c(g) \subset c(f)\) and \(c(f)\cap c(g) \subset c(f)\), we have that \(c(f)=A\) and \(c(g)=A\). So if \(fg\) is primitive then \(f\) is primitive and \(g\) is primitive.
If \(c(f)=A\) and \(c(g)=A\). Suppose \(C_{fg}\neq A\). Then by a fundamental property of commutative rings proved using Zorn’s lemma, there exists a maximal ideal containing \(C_{fg}\). Denote this ideal by \(\mathfrak m\). The quotient ring \(k_\mathfrak m = A/\mathfrak m\) is a field, called the residue field of \(\mathfrak m\). I think the name “residue field” stems from the case when \(A=\mathbb Z\) and \(\mathfrak m=(p)\), where \(p\) is a prime number. Then the “classes” in the quotient ring \(\mathbb Z/(p)\) are represented by the remainders modulo \(p\). These remainders are sometimes called the residues.
Consider the homomorphism \(A \to k_\mathfrak m\). This map extends naturally to the homomorphism \(A[x]\to k_\mathfrak m[x]\), such that \(\sum_{i=0}^n a_ix^i\mapsto \sum_{i=0}^n\overline{a_i}x^i.\) At this stage we have to check that this extension exists explicitly. At a higher level we can say the following: tensor the map \(A\to k_\mathfrak m\) by \(A[x]\) over \(A\). Note that the quotient \(k_\mathfrak m=A/\mathfrak m\) is a \(A\) module. So we have \[(A\to k_\mathfrak m)\otimes_A A[x] = A\otimes_ AA[x]\to k_\mathfrak m\otimes_A A[x] = A[X]\to k_\mathfrak m[x],\quad \sum_{i=0}^n a_ix^i\mapsto \sum_{i=0}^n\overline{a_i}x^i.\]
Under this homomorphism \(fg\) map to \(\overline{fg}\), which is equal to \(\overline{f}\cdot \overline{g}\), because this map is a homomorphism. Since the coefficients if \(fg\) are in \(\mathfrak m\), their image in \(k_\mathfrak m\) is \(0\). So the image of \(fg\) is \(0\) in \(k_\mathfrak m[x]\). As the coefficients of \(f\) generates the unit ideal, all the coefficients of \(f\) are not in \(\mathfrak m\), or else \(\mathfrak m\) would be \(A\). So there exists atleast one coefficient of \(f\), whose image in \(k_\mathfrak m\) is nonzero. Hence the image of \(f\), under this map will be nonzero. Similarly the image of \(g\) under this map would be nonzeo. So \(\overline{f}\) and \(\overline{g}\) are nonzero elements in \(k_\mathfrak m[x]\). But their product is \(\overline{fg}\), which is \(0\) in \(k_\mathfrak m[x]\). But this is not possible as \(k_\mathfrak m[x]\) is an integral domain because the coefficient field \(k_\mathfrak m\) is a field. So if \(c(f)=A\) and \(c(g)=A\), then we also must have \(C_{fg}=A\).
This completes the proof.
The proof of “\(f\) and \(g\) are primitive \(\Rightarrow\) \(fg\)” is primitive used a technique that is not transparent. It is very instructive to understand it and try to show expicitly that if some \(R-\)linear combination of the coefficients of \(f\) equals \(1\)(generates unity) and similarly some \(R-\) linear combination of the coefficients of \(g\) equals \(1\), then there exists an \(R-\) linear combination of the coefficients of \(fg\) that equal \(1\).

1. How Your Dynamic Identity System Works
By placing .gitconfig-profile inside ~/gits/randomnumberanonymous/, you have compartmentalized your Git profiles.
In your global configuration file (~/.gitconfig), you likely have a mechanism that functions exactly like this conditional layout:
# Global configurations for all repositories
[user]
    name = Biswajit Rajaguru
    email = default-email@example.com

# The magic conditional switch
[includeIf "gitdir:~/gits/randomnumberanonymous/"]
    path = ~/gits/randomnumberanonymous/.gitconfig-profile

The Symlink Advantage
Notice that math-blog inside your profile directory is a symlink pointing out to your true absolute workspace: math-blog -> /home/biswajitrajaguru/git/math-blog
Because Git resolves the absolute real path of a repository when you perform operations, as long as your conditional includes look at the final path or you use gitdir/i (case-insensitive/symlink-aware matching), Git automatically injects your account-specific overrides. Your specific profile file (.gitconfig-profile) tells Git to use your neutral SSH host alias:
[user]
    email = your-github-account-email@example.com

[url "git@github-randomnumberanonymous:randomnumberanonymous/"]
    insteadOf = git@github.com:randomnumberanonymous/
Because of that insteadOf block or your mapped remote, you never have to manually edit the SSH configuration strings whenever you clone or configure a new project. Git intercepts the network protocol layer on the fly.

2. Breaking Down the Cloud Pipeline (publish.yml)
When you execute git push -u origin main locally, the dynamic infrastructure shifts into the cloud. Your publish.yml GitHub Actions file instantly interprets your code and sets up a containerized Ubuntu runner.
Here is the exact step-by-step assembly line that triggers on GitHub’s architecture the second your push hits the server:

The Assembly Line Breakdown
on:
  push:
    branches: [ main, master ]

The Trigger: The runner sits dormant until it catches a git push event targeting either the main or master branches of your repo.

permissions:
  contents: write

Elevated Privileges: Because this workflow needs to programmatically compile HTML files and write them back down onto a separate deployment branch (gh-pages), you explicitly grant the temporary runner security authorization to write changes into your repository’s cloud tree.


The Three Sequential Steps:

actions/checkout@v4 The runner provisions a clean virtual machine (ubuntu-latest) and runs a local checkout clone inside it, pulling down all your raw .qmd files, your _quarto.yml, and your assets into the temporary server workspace.
quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2 Installs the full Quarto compilation engine directly onto the virtual server, updating any required underlying dependencies so it can process advanced scientific typesetting.
quarto-dev/quarto-actions/publish@v2 with target: gh-pages This is the heavy lifter. It runs the equivalent of quarto render in the cloud. It compiles your .qmd markdown files down to static web-native .html pages, processes your custom MathJax blocks, builds a hidden deployment directory, and dynamically pushes those static assets onto a background gh-pages branch.

GitHub Pages then seamlessly displays that compiled gh-pages output directly to the public web interface at https://randomnumberanonymous.github.io/math-blog/.
This setup gives you the ultimate professional developer environment: complete structural automation locally across your multiple profiles, and a robust cloud-compilation environment that guarantees your mathematical proofs render flawlessly down to the last symbol!

text:
What It Looks Like Under the Hood
When you use the -u flag, Git modifies your repository’s local configuration file (.git/config).
It adds a tracking block to the bottom of the file that looks like this:
[branch "main"]
    remote = origin
    merge = refs/heads/main
Without the -u flag, your files would still upload to GitHub, but Git wouldn’t create this tracking block. If you tried to type a plain git pull later, Git would stop you and say: “There is no tracking information for the current branch.”
Using -u is essentially a convenience feature that sets up short-command automation for the entire lifecycle of that branch!

Step 2: Configure Native MathJax

website:

    include-in-header:

              tex: {
                tags: 'ams',
                macros: {
                  \Spec: '\\text{Spec}',
                  \Proj: '\\text{Proj}',
                  \O: '\\mathcal{O}'
                }
              }
            };

website:

git remote add origin https://github.com/yourusername/math-solutions.git

name: Quarto Publish

The default WordPress block editor handles multi-line structural mathematics (like commutative diagrams, custom macros, or aligned proof environments) poorly.
To bypass this, Terence Tao writes his posts entirely offline on his computer as a standard compiled LaTeX document (.tex). He then uses a Python compilation script called latex2wp (originally written by computer scientist Luca Trevisan). 1. He writes and proofreads his post completely offline using a local LaTeX editor. 2. He runs the Python script on the .tex file. 3. The script translates math macros, labels, \ref{}, \eqref{}, and theorem environments into raw HTML shortcodes. 4. He copies that raw text, logs into the online WordPress dashboard, pastes it into the HTML editor, and publishes it.
This satisfies the offline requirement, but it isn’t “real-time browser preview” like StackExchange; it’s compiling a local PDF first.

If you want a native WordPress blog hosted completely for free with comments and MathJax, you cannot use the commercial WordPress.com free tier (as it blocks the necessary math plugins). You must use a free host or an alternative deployment model for self-hosted WordPress (WordPress.org).

1. The Rendering Engine (The Math Plugins)
To avoid ugly, unscalable PNG image equations, you need true vector math. You must install one of these free plugins: * Simple MathJax: Allows you to use standard $ and $$ delimiters anywhere on your site. It injects the MathJax script natively, allowing readers to right-click formulas, zoom, or copy the raw LaTeX code. * WP QuickLaTeX: An advanced engine that allows you to define a custom LaTeX preamble directly inside WordPress. This is essential for advanced mathematics because it lets you globally load amsmath, amssymb, or custom shorthand macros (like \newcommand{\Spec}{\text{Spec}}).


2. The Comment System
WordPress has an incredibly robust, native, multi-threaded comment and reply system built into every theme out of the box. No external configurations are needed for readers to comment.

The Major Catch: The Compromises
While WordPress provides a polished UI, it forces hard tradeoffs for your specific criteria:

❌ No True Offline-to-Online Syncing
WordPress stores all posts, categories, and settings inside an online relational database (MySQL). It is not file-backed. You cannot simply save a folder of text files offline and run a command to push them to your server. To write offline, you either have to: * Draft in a separate text editor offline and manually copy-paste when you are back online. * Set up a complete local server stack (like Docker or LocalWP) on your Fedora system to run an entire separate copy of WordPress offline, and then manually export/import the database files to sync them—which is an incredibly tedious workflow for a single math blog.


❌ Subpar Live Math Preview
The modern WordPress block editor (Gutenberg) does not feature an integrated, zero-latency side-by-side math compiler like MathOverflow. While some plugins try to offer block previews, heavy sheets of mathematical proofs with nested fractions, matrices, and custom alignments will frequently lag or throw block errors in the visual dashboard.

mkdir -p ~/opt
tar -C ~/opt -xvzf quarto-1.9.38-linux-amd64.tar.gz

mkdir -p ~/.local/bin
ln -s ~/opt/quarto-1.9.38/bin/quarto ~/.local/bin/quarto

# 4. Bind it permanently to your environment shell path
if [[ ":$PATH:" != *":$HOME/.local/bin:"* ]]; then
    echo 'export PATH="$PATH:$HOME/.local/bin"' >> ~/.bashrc
    source ~/.bashrc
fi

# Verification step (Should spit out the current tracking version)
quarto --version


For a Windows Contingency Machine
If you have to drop down into a Windows terminal layer later, install Git for Windows, then open PowerShell and run:
winget install --id Posit.Quarto

Step 4: Handle Seamless Password/Token Authentication
GitHub disabled standard account passwords for terminal tasks, requiring Personal Access Tokens (PATs) instead. To prevent Account One’s credentials from colliding with Account Two’s credentials on the same machine, inject your specific username directly into the repository’s remote URL structure.
When you clone a repository or update an existing remote path, format it explicitly with the targeted username:
# Form a fresh clone using an explicit profile target:
git clone https://username_one@github.com/username_one/math-blog.git

# Or fix an existing repository path inside its root folder:
git remote set-url origin https://username_one@github.com/username_one/math-blog.git

Why this works across all machines (Linux & Windows)

When you type git push, Git reads username_one@github.com.
Your system’s native secure password storage (GCM/Secret Service on Linux, or Windows Credential Manager) isolates this distinct lookup handle.
The first time you push, it will ask for a password. Paste the Personal Access Token generated from that specific account.
Your OS will securely lock that token to only match that specific username. You will never have to provide it on that computer again, and your two profiles will never accidentally cross-authenticate each other.

1. What is ~/.gitconfig?
This is your Global Configuration File. It is written in the standard INI format and lives directly at the root of your home directory (~).

The Scope: It serves as the catch-all, default baseline for your entire machine user account. If a specific local repository does not explicitly declare a custom setting, it inherits the rule straight from this file.
The Role in your Multi-Account Setup: It is the “Traffic Controller.” It sets up your general fallbacks, but its most critical job right now is holding the conditional redirection rules:
[includeIf "gitdir:~/gits/account_one/"]
    path = ~/gits/account_one/.gitconfig-profile

2. What is ~/gits/account_one/.gitconfig-profile?
This is a Custom Supplemental Profile File that you manually created. It is structurally identical to a standard configuration file but lacks any default tracking status.

The Scope: It has zero effect on its own. Git does not scan your file system looking for files named .gitconfig-profile.
The Activation Engine: It only wakes up when the traffic controller inside ~/.gitconfig reads its conditional match requirement. When your terminal is active inside ~/gits/account_one/, Git dynamically injects the contents of this supplemental file directly on top of your global settings, overriding your fallback email and name in memory.

3. The Cascading Layers of Git Logic
When you execute a command like git commit, Git queries its configuration values by flattening down multiple text files in a precise hierarchy from lowest priority to highest priority:
[ Layer 1: System Level ]       --> /etc/gitconfig (Applies to all OS users)
           ↓
[ Layer 2: Global Level ]       --> ~/.gitconfig (Your primary user baselines)
           ↓
[ Layer 3: Conditional Level ]  --> Activated dynamically by [includeIf] paths
           ↓
[ Layer 4: Local Level ]        --> your-project/.git/config (Inside the hidden repo folder)
If a setting (like user.email) is defined in multiple layers, the highest layer wins. —

4. The Effect of the git config Command
When you type configuration adjustments into your terminal, the presence or absence of flags dictates exactly which text file layer on your hard drive is opened and modified:

Case A: Running with --global
git config --global user.email "math@example.com"

The Effect: This targets Layer 2. Git opens ~/.gitconfig directly and writes or updates the lines under the [user] block. This rule will now dictate the behavior for every repository on your machine—unless overridden by a higher layer.



Case B: Running without --global (Local Repository Scope)
cd ~/gits/account_one/math-blog
git config user.email "hartshorne-solutions@example.com"

The Effect: This targets Layer 4. Git completely skips your global file and writes the setting directly inside the hidden .git/config file belonging only to that specific project folder.
The Trap: If you run this command inside math-blog, it will permanently lock that email to that folder, rendering your elegant includeIf directory scanning script useless for this specific repository because Local overrides Conditional. To let your profile files handle the swapping automatically, you should avoid dropping local directory overrides.

Quarto actually supports environment-based overrides, but the cleanest way to handle this without maintaining two separate _quarto.yml files is using a simple local profile.


Step 1: Set up a Profile for Local Offline Preview
In the same folder as your main _quarto.yml, create a new file named _quarto-offline.yml:
# _quarto-offline.yml
format:
  html:
    self-contained-math: true
That’s all that goes in it! Quarto will merge this file with your main _quarto.yml whenever you activate the offline profile.



Step 2: Keep your Main Configuration Default (CDN)

# _quarto.yml

format:

Step 3: How You Run It

1. When working offline locally:
Run your preview using the --profile flag:
quarto preview --profile offline

What happens: Quarto merges _quarto-offline.yml into _quarto.yml. It fetches/uses the local bundled MathJax assets so all your equations render instantly without an internet connection.



2. When GitHub Actions publishes your live site:
When you run git push origin main, your GitHub Actions workflow runs the default build command (quarto publish / quarto render).

What happens: Since GitHub Actions doesn’t pass --profile offline, it uses only _quarto.yml. It compiles your blog linking directly to the high-speed CDN JS files!

What is the .github/ folder?
In the world of Git and GitHub, any folder or file that begins with a dot (like .gitignore or .github/) is a hidden directory. By convention, GitHub reserves the specialized .github/ folder at the absolute root of your project repository to hold all configuration files related to GitHub’s automated features, project management, and server-side logic.
If you put configuration files anywhere else in your project, GitHub’s servers will completely ignore them.



What is the workflows/ folder?
Inside that .github/ directory sits a mandatory subfolder named workflows/.
This folder is the dedicated command center for GitHub Actions (GitHub’s built-in automation and continuous integration platform). Every single .yml or .yaml file you place inside .github/workflows/ acts as an independent script telling GitHub’s cloud servers to spin up an isolated virtual machine and execute tasks on your behalf whenever specific triggers occur.



How publish.yml Triggers Actions
Your publish.yml file is written in YAML (Yet Another Markup Language). It functions exactly like a blueprint or a recipe. GitHub’s servers constantly monitor your repository, and the moment a condition inside that file is met, it parses the instructions from top to bottom.
Here is the exact mechanism of how your publish.yml orchestrates a build:

1. The Event Listener (on:)
At the very top of your file, you have this block:
on:
  push:
    branches: [ main, master ]
GitHub reads this as an active webhook listener. The split second you execute git push origin main from your Fedora terminal and the code lands on GitHub’s servers, GitHub flags a Push Event. It checks .github/workflows/ for any script listening for a push to the main branch, finds your publish.yml, and triggers the workflow run.


2. Provisioning the Environment (runs-on:)
jobs:
  build-deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
GitHub allocates a clean, isolated cloud virtual machine (a “runner”) running the latest version of Ubuntu Linux.


3. Step-by-Step Execution (steps:)
The runner executes a sequence of isolated actions down the file line-by-line:

Step A (uses: actions/checkout@v4): The clean Ubuntu virtual machine starts completely empty. This step clones your repository’s files (_quarto.yml, your .qmd notebooks, your books/ folder) directly onto the virtual machine’s local hard drive so it can work on them.
Step B (uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2): This downloads and installs the Quarto CLI engine onto the cloud virtual machine, making the quarto command available in its environment.
Step C (uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/publish@v2): This acts exactly as if someone typed quarto publish gh-pages directly into a terminal on that cloud machine. Quarto compiles your markdown and mathematical notation into production HTML/CSS assets and immediately commits and pushes those generated files over onto your repository’s isolated gh-pages branch.

Once the final step finishes without throwing a terminal error, the virtual machine safely dissolves, and GitHub updates your dashboard with a green checkmark!
quarto publish gh-pages means dump the published html/css/ etc into the gh-pages golder? which is accessible online
Exactly! You’ve got the concept down perfectly, though there is one subtle but brilliant Git trick happening under the hood that makes it even cooler than a regular folder.
When you run quarto publish gh-pages, Quarto doesn’t just dump the files into a local folder named gh-pages. Instead, it treats gh-pages as a completely separate branch (like a parallel timeline of your project) that lives hidden inside your .git database.
Here is exactly how it splits the work behind the scenes:



The Two Parallel Timelines
               [ Your Repository ]
                       |
        +--------------+--------------+
        |                             |
    [ main branch ]             [ gh-pages branch ]
  Your raw source code:        The compiled website:
  - index.qmd                  - index.html
  - _quarto.yml                - site_libs/
  - books/ (.qmd files)        - books/ (.html files)




What Quarto Does in that Split Second
When that step runs, Quarto acts like a lightning-fast digital assistant:

It reads your raw .qmd files on the main branch.
It compiles all your text and complex mathematical symbols into static html, css, and javascript assets inside a temporary scratchpad.
It sneaks behind the scenes, switches over to your empty gh-pages branch, cracks open that snapshot, drops only those compiled web files there, and seals a brand-new commit.
It fires a git push origin gh-pages to launch that specific branch straight to GitHub’s cloud servers.




Why is it Accessible Online?
GitHub is hardwired to watch that specific gh-pages branch if you turn on GitHub Pages in your settings.
The moment GitHub’s native web servers see a new commit land on gh-pages, they immediately grab that raw index.html file and serve it up instantly to any web browser requesting your URL ([https://randomnumberanonymous.github.io/math-blog/](https://randomnumberanonymous.github.io/math-blog/)).
It’s an incredibly clean separation: your main branch stays pristine with just your clean markdown text and geometry notes, while your gh-pages branch does all the messy work of hosting the heavy compiled code!

Quarto includes MathJax rendering by default. In your global configuration file (_quarto.yml), you can easily define your standard LaTeX packages or macro shortcuts so they are accessible across all solution posts:
website:
  title: "Spec(R): Math Notes"
  
format:
  html:
    theme: cosmo
    html-math-method: mathjax
    include-in-header:
      - text: |
          <script>
            window.MathJax = {
              tex: {
                tags: 'ams',
                macros: {
                  \Spec: '\\text{Spec}',
                  \Proj: '\\text{Proj}',
                  \O: '\\mathcal{O}'
                }
              }
            };
          </script>

Let $X = \Spec(R)$ be an affine scheme. The structure sheaf $\O_X$ satisfies...

$$
\Gamma(X, \O_X) \cong R
$$


Step 3: Add the Commenting System (Giscus)
Since your blog is static, you don’t host a database for comments. Instead, you can leverage Giscus, a system that uses GitHub Discussions as a backend. * Visitors can log in via GitHub and reply directly to your posts. * The comments load beautifully on your static pages via a lightweight JavaScript snippet. * To set it up, you just need to make a public GitHub repository, enable the “Discussions” feature on it, and install the Giscus app. Quarto has direct configuration support for this in your _quarto.yml:
website:
  comments:
    giscus:
      repo: yourusername/math-solutions


Step 4: Host Online for Free via GitHub Pages

Create a public repository on GitHub named math-solutions (or yourusername.github.io).
Link your local project to GitHub:
git remote add origin https://github.com/yourusername/math-solutions.git
Set up GitHub Actions to automate publishing. When you push your raw text documents, GitHub’s servers will automatically build the site. You can add a simple workflow file under .github/workflows/publish.yml:

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]
name: Quarto Publish
jobs:
  build-deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write
    steps:
      - name: Check out repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Set up Quarto
        uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2
      - name: Publish to GitHub Pages
        uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/publish@v2
        with:
          target: gh-pages

How Terence Tao Does It (latex2wp)
The default WordPress block editor handles multi-line structural mathematics (like commutative diagrams, custom macros, or aligned proof environments) poorly.
To bypass this, Terence Tao writes his posts entirely offline on his computer as a standard compiled LaTeX document (.tex). He then uses a Python compilation script called latex2wp (originally written by computer scientist Luca Trevisan). 1. He writes and proofreads his post completely offline using a local LaTeX editor. 2. He runs the Python script on the .tex file. 3. The script translates math macros, labels, \ref{}, \eqref{}, and theorem environments into raw HTML shortcodes. 4. He copies that raw text, logs into the online WordPress dashboard, pastes it into the HTML editor, and publishes it.
This satisfies the offline requirement, but it isn’t “real-time browser preview” like StackExchange; it’s compiling a local PDF first.

2. The Comment System

The Major Catch: The Compromises
While WordPress provides a polished UI, it forces hard tradeoffs for your specific criteria:

❌ No True Offline-to-Online Syncing
WordPress stores all posts, categories, and settings inside an online relational database (MySQL). It is not file-backed. You cannot simply save a folder of text files offline and run a command to push them to your server. To write offline, you either have to: * Draft in a separate text editor offline and manually copy-paste when you are back online. * Set up a complete local server stack (like Docker or LocalWP) on your Fedora system to run an entire separate copy of WordPress offline, and then manually export/import the database files to sync them—which is an incredibly tedious workflow for a single math blog.


❌ Subpar Live Math Preview
The modern WordPress block editor (Gutenberg) does not feature an integrated, zero-latency side-by-side math compiler like MathOverflow. While some plugins try to offer block previews, heavy sheets of mathematical proofs with nested fractions, matrices, and custom alignments will frequently lag or throw block errors in the visual dashboard.

Phase 2: Local Workspace Environment Configuration
Because you swap between distribution ecosystems (and even Windows), use a tarball/standalone package approach rather than system-level package managers wherever possible to ensure exact parity across environments.

For Fedora (i3 Spin) & Debian/Ubuntu
Run this setup to safely manage your system pathways without needing sudo rights or messing with system packages:
# 1. Pull down the standalone Linux tarball
wget https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/releases/download/v1.9.38/quarto-1.9.38-linux-amd64.tar.gz

# 2. Extract into a localized application bin
mkdir -p ~/opt
tar -C ~/opt -xvzf quarto-1.9.38-linux-amd64.tar.gz

# 3. Form a clean link inside your user path space
mkdir -p ~/.local/bin
ln -s ~/opt/quarto-1.9.38/bin/quarto ~/.local/bin/quarto

# 4. Bind it permanently to your environment shell path
if [[ ":$PATH:" != *":$HOME/.local/bin:"* ]]; then
    echo 'export PATH="$PATH:$HOME/.local/bin"' >> ~/.bashrc
    source ~/.bashrc
fi

# Verification step (Should spit out the current tracking version)
quarto --version


For a Windows Contingency Machine
If you have to drop down into a Windows terminal layer later, install Git for Windows, then open PowerShell and run:
winget install --id Posit.Quarto
Because your structure relies entirely on standard markdown text configurations, both your text paths and layouts operate identically regardless of your base operating system.

Step 4: Handle Seamless Password/Token Authentication
GitHub disabled standard account passwords for terminal tasks, requiring Personal Access Tokens (PATs) instead. To prevent Account One’s credentials from colliding with Account Two’s credentials on the same machine, inject your specific username directly into the repository’s remote URL structure.
When you clone a repository or update an existing remote path, format it explicitly with the targeted username:
# Form a fresh clone using an explicit profile target:
git clone https://username_one@github.com/username_one/math-blog.git

# Or fix an existing repository path inside its root folder:
git remote set-url origin https://username_one@github.com/username_one/math-blog.git

Why this works across all machines (Linux & Windows)

When you type git push, Git reads username_one@github.com.
Your system’s native secure password storage (GCM/Secret Service on Linux, or Windows Credential Manager) isolates this distinct lookup handle.
The first time you push, it will ask for a password. Paste the Personal Access Token generated from that specific account.
Your OS will securely lock that token to only match that specific username. You will never have to provide it on that computer again, and your two profiles will never accidentally cross-authenticate each other.

href: how I created this blog/How I creaed this blog v2.html#what-is-.gitconfig
title: you asked
text:
1. What is ~/.gitconfig?
This is your Global Configuration File. It is written in the standard INI format and lives directly at the root of your home directory (~).

The Scope: It serves as the catch-all, default baseline for your entire machine user account. If a specific local repository does not explicitly declare a custom setting, it inherits the rule straight from this file.
The Role in your Multi-Account Setup: It is the “Traffic Controller.” It sets up your general fallbacks, but its most critical job right now is holding the conditional redirection rules:
[includeIf "gitdir:~/gits/account_one/"]
    path = ~/gits/account_one/.gitconfig-profile

objectID: how I created this blog/How I creaed this blog v2.html#what-is-gitsaccount_one.gitconfig-profile
href: how I created this blog/How I creaed this blog v2.html#what-is-gitsaccount_one.gitconfig-profile
title: you asked
text:
2. What is ~/gits/account_one/.gitconfig-profile?
This is a Custom Supplemental Profile File that you manually created. It is structurally identical to a standard configuration file but lacks any default tracking status.

The Scope: It has zero effect on its own. Git does not scan your file system looking for files named .gitconfig-profile.
The Activation Engine: It only wakes up when the traffic controller inside ~/.gitconfig reads its conditional match requirement. When your terminal is active inside ~/gits/account_one/, Git dynamically injects the contents of this supplemental file directly on top of your global settings, overriding your fallback email and name in memory.

href: how I created this blog/How I creaed this blog v2.html#the-cascading-layers-of-git-logic

section: 3. The Cascading Layers of Git Logic
text:
3. The Cascading Layers of Git Logic
When you execute a command like git commit, Git queries its configuration values by flattening down multiple text files in a precise hierarchy from lowest priority to highest priority:
[ Layer 1: System Level ]       --> /etc/gitconfig (Applies to all OS users)
           ↓
[ Layer 2: Global Level ]       --> ~/.gitconfig (Your primary user baselines)
           ↓
[ Layer 3: Conditional Level ]  --> Activated dynamically by [includeIf] paths
           ↓
[ Layer 4: Local Level ]        --> your-project/.git/config (Inside the hidden repo folder)
If a setting (like user.email) is defined in multiple layers, the highest layer wins. —

section: 4. The Effect of the git config Command
text:
4. The Effect of the git config Command
When you type configuration adjustments into your terminal, the presence or absence of flags dictates exactly which text file layer on your hard drive is opened and modified:

Case A: Running with --global
git config --global user.email "math@example.com"

The Effect: This targets Layer 2. Git opens ~/.gitconfig directly and writes or updates the lines under the [user] block. This rule will now dictate the behavior for every repository on your machine—unless overridden by a higher layer.



Case B: Running without --global (Local Repository Scope)
cd ~/gits/account_one/math-blog
git config user.email "hartshorne-solutions@example.com"

The Effect: This targets Layer 4. Git completely skips your global file and writes the setting directly inside the hidden .git/config file belonging only to that specific project folder.
The Trap: If you run this command inside math-blog, it will permanently lock that email to that folder, rendering your elegant includeIf directory scanning script useless for this specific repository because Local overrides Conditional. To let your profile files handle the swapping automatically, you should avoid dropping local directory overrides.

text:
The Final Milestone: Secure Token Authentication (PAT)
Since GitHub does not accept your standard account password when pushing code from a terminal, you need to issue a secure Personal Access Token (Classic). This will act as the master key for your randomnumberanonymous profile on this machine.

Step 1: Generate the Token on GitHub

Log into your randomnumberanonymous account on GitHub.
Click your profile picture in the top-right corner \(\rightarrow\) Settings.
Scroll all the way down the left-hand sidebar and click Developer settings.
In the left sidebar, click Personal access tokens \(\rightarrow\) Tokens (classic).
Click the Generate new token dropdown and select Generate new token (classic).
Configure the token:

Note: Give it a clear descriptive label like: Fedora Linux Laptop Token.
Expiration: Set it to 90 days, 180 days, or “No expiration” depending on your preference.
Scopes (Permissions): Check the box next to repo (this grants full control over your private and public repositories, which is required to push your blog code and let the Actions automation run).

Scroll to the bottom and click the green Generate token button.

⚠️ CRITICAL: Copy the long token string (it usually starts with ghp_) immediately. GitHub will never show it to you again. Paste it safely into a local scratch file or a secure password manager temporary note.



Step 2: Push and Save the Token
Now, let’s tie it all together and publish your blog live to the world. Ensure you are inside your local directory:
cd ~/git/math-blog
Run your first push command:
git push origin main
Your terminal will pause and ask you for inputs: 1. Username: Type your literal account handle: randomnumberanonymous. 2. Password: Do not type your account password. text:
1. How Your Dynamic Identity System Works
By placing .gitconfig-profile inside ~/gits/randomnumberanonymous/, you have compartmentalized your Git profiles.
In your global configuration file (~/.gitconfig), you likely have a mechanism that functions exactly like this conditional layout:
# Global configurations for all repositories
[user]
    name = Biswajit Rajaguru
    email = default-email@example.com

# The magic conditional switch
[includeIf "gitdir:~/gits/randomnumberanonymous/"]
    path = ~/gits/randomnumberanonymous/.gitconfig-profile

The Symlink Advantage
Notice that math-blog inside your profile directory is a symlink pointing out to your true absolute workspace: math-blog -> /home/biswajitrajaguru/git/math-blog
Because Git resolves the absolute real path of a repository when you perform operations, as long as your conditional includes look at the final path or you use gitdir/i (case-insensitive/symlink-aware matching), Git automatically injects your account-specific overrides. Your specific profile file (.gitconfig-profile) tells Git to use your neutral SSH host alias:
[user]
    email = your-github-account-email@example.com

[url "git@github-randomnumberanonymous:randomnumberanonymous/"]
    insteadOf = git@github.com:randomnumberanonymous/
Because of that insteadOf block or your mapped remote, you never have to manually edit the SSH configuration strings whenever you clone or configure a new project. Git intercepts the network protocol layer on the fly.

text:
2. Breaking Down the Cloud Pipeline (publish.yml)
When you execute git push -u origin main locally, the dynamic infrastructure shifts into the cloud. Your publish.yml GitHub Actions file instantly interprets your code and sets up a containerized Ubuntu runner.
Here is the exact step-by-step assembly line that triggers on GitHub’s architecture the second your push hits the server:

The Assembly Line Breakdown
on:
  push:
    branches: [ main, master ]

The Trigger: The runner sits dormant until it catches a git push event targeting either the main or master branches of your repo.

permissions:
  contents: write

Elevated Privileges: Because this workflow needs to programmatically compile HTML files and write them back down onto a separate deployment branch (gh-pages), you explicitly grant the temporary runner security authorization to write changes into your repository’s cloud tree.


The Three Sequential Steps:

actions/checkout@v4 The runner provisions a clean virtual machine (ubuntu-latest) and runs a local checkout clone inside it, pulling down all your raw .qmd files, your _quarto.yml, and your assets into the temporary server workspace.
quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2 Installs the full Quarto compilation engine directly onto the virtual server, updating any required underlying dependencies so it can process advanced scientific typesetting.
quarto-dev/quarto-actions/publish@v2 with target: gh-pages This is the heavy lifter. It runs the equivalent of quarto render in the cloud. It compiles your .qmd markdown files down to static web-native .html pages, processes your custom MathJax blocks, builds a hidden deployment directory, and dynamically pushes those static assets onto a background gh-pages branch.

GitHub Pages then seamlessly displays that compiled gh-pages output directly to the public web interface at https://randomnumberanonymous.github.io/math-blog/.
This setup gives you the ultimate professional developer environment: complete structural automation locally across your multiple profiles, and a robust cloud-compilation environment that guarantees your mathematical proofs render flawlessly down to the last symbol!

Why Use It?
You only need to use the -u flag the very first time you push a new branch to a remote server.
Once that tracking link is established, Git remembers the relationship. For all future updates on that branch, you no longer need to type the remote name or the branch name. You can simply type:
git push

git pull

section: What It Looks Like Under the Hood
text:
What It Looks Like Under the Hood
When you use the -u flag, Git modifies your repository’s local configuration file (.git/config).
It adds a tracking block to the bottom of the file that looks like this:
[branch "main"]
    remote = origin
    merge = refs/heads/main
Without the -u flag, your files would still upload to GitHub, but Git wouldn’t create this tracking block. If you tried to type a plain git pull later, Git would stop you and say: “There is no tracking information for the current branch.”
Using -u is essentially a convenience feature that sets up short-command automation for the entire lifecycle of that branch!

objectID: books/Atiyah McDonald Commutative Algebra/1. Rings and Ideals/Exercises/1/1.html#question

text: Let \(x\) be a nilpotent element of a ring \(A\). Show that \(1+x\) is a unit of \(A\). Deduce that the sum of a nilpotent element and an unit is a unit.

objectID: books/Atiyah McDonald Commutative Algebra/1. Rings and Ideals/Exercises/1/1.html#solution
href: books/Atiyah McDonald Commutative Algebra/1. Rings and Ideals/Exercises/1/1.html#solution
text:
Solution
Fact: If \(x\) is a nilpotent element of a ring, then the infinite sum \(\displaystyle y =\sum_{n=0}^\infty x^n\) is well defined as an element of the ring \(A\). This element is a unit of \(A\) and \(\displaystyle (1-x)(\sum_{n=0}^\infty x^n) = 1\).
Proof: Let \(x^{N+1}=0\). Then \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty x^n = 1+\cdots+x^N\).
So \(\displaystyle (1-x)(\sum_{n=0}^\infty x^n) = (1-x)(1+\cdots+x^N) = (1+\cdots+x^N)-(x+\cdots+x^{N+1}) = 1 - x^{N+1} = 1.\)
If \(x\) is nilpotent, then \(-x\) is also nilpotent. In particular if \(x^N=0\), then \((-x)^N=0\). So the above proof implies: \[\big(1-(-x)\big)\big(\sum_{n=0}^\infty (-x)^n\big) = 1.\]
Hence \((1+x)\big(1-x+x^2-\cdots+(-1)^Nx^N\big)=1\).
Let us now consider the generalisation. Suppose \(u\) is an unit of \(A\) and \(n\) is a nilpotent element of \(A\). Let \(s = u + n\). Now to use the result we just proved we have to some way relate it to a sum of the form \(1+x\). There are two facts:
(a). The product of a nilpotent element with any other element is also nilpotent.
(b). If \(v\) is an unit, then an element \(a\) of the ring is an unit if and only if the element \(va\) is also an unit.
So to prove that \(u+n\) is a unit it is sufficient to prove \(v(u+n)\) is also an unit for some unit \(v\). We want the product \(v(u+n)\) to be of the form \(1+x\), where \(x\) is nilpotent. The most suggestive candidate for \(v\) is \(u^{-1}\). But \(u^{-1}(u+n)=1+u^{-1}n\). This last sum is of the form \(1+x\), with \(x\) nilpotent. So this sum is an unit. Hence the original sum is an unit.
Almost every exercise in this book teaches us an important fact, that we need to remember. When working in Algebraic geometry all these facts are very useful. In fact that is the purpose of the exercises, particularly in this book.
The first fact to remember is that the sum and difference of a unit and nilpotent is an unit. So \(\pm u \pm n\) is a unit keeping in mind that \(-1\) is a unit in any ring.
Fact: the sum of two nilpotents is nilpotent.
Proof: Let \(a^{n_1}=0\) and \(b^{n_2}=0\). Then \(\displaystyle (a+b)^{n_1+n_2-1} = \sum_{i+j=n_1+n_2-1}a^ib^j\). But if \(i\leq n_1-1\), then \(j = n_1+n_2-1-i=n_2 + (n_1-1-i)\geq n_2\). So in every summand of this binomial sum the power of \(a\) is atleast \(n_1\) or the power of \(b\) is atleast \(n_2\). So in all summands either the power of \(a\) is \(0\) or the power of \(b\) is \(0\). So every summand is \(0\). So the sum \(0\). Hence \((a+b)^{n_1+n_2-1}=0\).
It is instructive verify these facts(that hold in commutative rings ) for square matrices, with entries in commutative rings. If \(R\) is a commutative ring, then \(M_n(R)\) denotes the ring of \(n\times n\) matrices with coefficients in \(R\). \(M_n(R)\) has a subring \(RI_n\) that lies at the center of the matrix ring, and \(M_n(R)\) is a \(R-\)algebra.
(a). If \(A\) is nilpotent, then \(I+A\) is a unit. The proof of this is same as that of first part above. This is because the sub-algebra(sub-ring) generated by \(A\) over \(R\) in \(M_n(R)\) is a commutative ring and all computations occur in this commutative ring. This ring is the image of \(R[x]\) under the homomorphism \(R[x]\to M_n(R),\quad x\mapsto A\).
(b). If \(A\) is nilpotent, and \(B\) is another matrix. Then \(AB\) maynot be nilpotent. Consider \[A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad B = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}.\] Then \(A\) is strictly upper-triangular, so it is nilpotent (\(A^2 = 0\)).\(B\) is strictly lower-triangular, so it is also nilpotent (\(B^2 = 0\)).Now let’s compute the product \(AB\):\[AB = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}.\] The product is a diagonal matrix with units in the diagonal. Such a matrix cannot be nilpotent. In fact a finite diagonal matrix is nilpotent iff the entries of the diagonal are nilpotent. So product of two nilpotents can be non-nilpotent.
(c). If \(N\) is a nilpotent matrix and \(A\) commutes with N, the \(AN\) is nilpotent. A pair of commuting matrices generates a commutative sub ring over the base ring. So all computations involving only them is done in that commutative ring. So properties that hold in commutative rings also holds good here.
(d). It is true that \(A\) is a unit iff there exists another unit \(B\), such that \(AB\) is a unit.
(e). The sum of unit and nilpotent need not be a unit in matrices. \[N = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix},U = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}.\] Then \[U + N =\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\] which is not invertible as its determinant is \(0\).
(f). But if \(U\) and \(N\) commute, then \(U^{-1}\) and \(N\) also commute . So that \(U^{-1}(U+N) = I + U^{-1}N\), But \(U^{-1}N\) is nilpotent by what we have said above. So \(I + U^{-1}N\) is an unit by what we have said before. So if \(U,N\) commute then \(U+N\) is an unit.

Exercise 1.1 (a)
Let \(Y\) be the plane curve \(y=x^2\) (i.e., \(Y\) is the zero set of the polynomial \(f=y-x^2\) ). Show that \(A(Y)\) is isomorphic to a polynomial ring in one variable over \(k\).


Solution:
Here \(f\) is a polynomial in \(k[x,y]\). Polynomials in \(k[x,y]\) are polynomials in the variables \(x\) and \(y\). We can evaluate such a polynomial when \(x\) has the value \(x_0\) and \(y\) has the value \(y_0\) where \(x_0,y_0\) are elements of the field \(k\) to get \(f(x_0,y_0)\) which is also an element of \(k\).
So given a polynomial in \(k[x,y]\), it can be evaluated at a point \(p_0=(x_0,y_0)\) in \(\mathbb A^2_k\) to get a value in \(k\). This process gives a map \[Eval_{p_0}:k[x,y]\to k, \quad g\mapsto g(p_0).\] This map is often called the evaluation map at the point \(p_0\). There is an algebraic way to get this map.
Let \(p_0\) denote the point \((x_0,y_0)\) in \(\mathbb A^2_k\). Consider the ideal \(\mathfrak m_{p_0} = (x-x_0,y-y_0)\). This is the ideal generated by the linear polynomials \(x-x_0\), and \(y-y_0\). We have:
The set of all polynomials that vanish at the point \(p_0=(p_{x_0},p_{y_0})\) is exactly the ideal \(\mathfrak m_{p_0}\).
Proof: Let \(u = x - p_{x_0}\) and \(v = y - p_{y_0}\). Then \(u\) and \(v\) are polynomials in \(k[x,y]\). Given a polynomial \(g(x,y)\) we can write it as polynomial in \(u\) and \(v\), by writing \(g(x,y)=g(u+p_{x_0},v+p_{y_0})\) and expanding the RHS. When the RHS is expanded we get a polynomial \(h(u,v)\) in \(u,v\). The polynomial \(g(x,y)\) and \(h(u,v)\) are the same element of the ring \(k[x,y]\). \[g \Bigg |_{x=p_{x_0},y=p_{y_0}} = h\Bigg |_{u=0,v=0}.\] So the constant term of the polynomial \(h\) is \(g(p_{x_0},p_{y_0})\). Hence we can write \(h(u,v)\) as \(uh_1(u,v)+vh_2(u,v)+g(p_{x_0},p_{y_0})\) for some polynomials \(h_1\) and \(h_2\). Since \(g(x,y)=h(u,v)\), we have that \(g(x,y)=(x-p_{x_0})h_1(u,v) + (y-p_{y_0})h_2(u,v) + g(p_{x_0},p_{y_0})\). So \(g(x,y)-g(p_{x_0},p_{y_0})\in \mathfrak m_{p_0}\).
If \(g(p_{x_0},p_{y_0})=0\), then \(g(x,y)\in\mathfrak m_{p_0}\). Conversely if \(g(x,y)\in\mathfrak m_{p_0}\), then \(g(p_{x_0},p_{y_0}) = 0\) as \((p_{x_0},p_{y_0})\) is a common zero of the generators \(x-p_{x_0},y-p_{y_0}\) of \(\mathfrak m_{p_0}\).
So \(I(\{p_0\}) = \mathfrak m_{p_0}\).
Fact: If \(R\) is a \(k-\)algebra for a field \(k\), and \(I\) is a proper ideal of \(R\). Then the quotient ring homomorphism \(R\to R/I\) gives the structure of a \(k-\)algebra to \(R/I\). In particular the quotient map is identity on \(k\subset R\).
Consider the following map:
\[k[x,y]\to k[x,y]/\mathfrak m_{p_0},\quad f\mapsto \overline{f}\]
As the zero set of \(\mathfrak m_{p_0}\) is nonempty, it does not contain any nonzero constant, because a non zero constant has empty zero set. So the above map is a \(k-\)algebra map and its restriction to \(k\) is injective. Also if \(f\in k[x,y]\), then \(f-f(p_0)\in\mathfrak m_{p_0}\). So \(\overline{f-f(p_0)} = 0\). So \(\overline{f} =\overline{f(p_0)}\). So we can say \(f\mapsto \overline{f(p_0)}\). As the above map is surjective, we have that the image of \(k[x,y]\) is same as the image of \(k\) under the above map. Hence the image is exactly \(k\). Please note here we are identifying the images of elements of \(k\in k[x,y]\) with their images in the quotient. With this identification \(\overline f = f(p_0)\).
So the value of \(f\) evaluated at \(p_0\) is the image of \(f\) under the quotient map \[k[x,y]\to k[x,y]/\mathfrak m_{p_0}.\].
This is how “Evaluation at \(p_0\)” can be intrepreted algebraically.
Fact: Since the quotient of \(\mathfrak m_{p_0}\) is a field, the ideal \(\mathfrak m_{p_0}\) must be a maximal ideal of a \(k[x,y]\).
All these things that we have seen in \(2-\)variables also holds good for the \(n-\)variable case.
Facts:

If \(f_1,\ldots,f_k\) generate an ideal \(I\) in \(k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), then \(Z(I)=Z(\{f_1,\ldots,f_k\})\).
Let \(g(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) and \(p_0=(p_{1_0},\ldots,p_{n_0})\in\mathbb A^n_k\). Then \(g(x_1,\ldots,x_n)-g(p_{1_0},\ldots,p_{n_0})\in\mathfrak m_{p_0}\). and \(I(\{(p_{1_0},\ldots,p_{n_0})\})=\mathfrak m_{p_0}\) The proof of this fact is the extension of the proof given above for the \(2-\)variable case to the \(n-\)variable case.
If \(p_0\in \mathbb A^n_k\), then \(\mathfrak m_{p_0}\) is a maximal ideal of \(k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\).

Note: We have not used that \(k\) is algebraically closed in the above discussion. Hence all this holds for non algebraically closed fields also.
\(Y:=\{p\in\mathbb A^2_k:f(p)=0\}\). Elements of \(k[x,y]\) are seen as functions on \(\mathbb A^2_k\). \(A(Y)\) is the set of functions we get by restricting the functions on \(\mathbb A^2_k\) to \(Y\). There is a natural map \[k[x,y]\to A(x,y),\quad f\mapsto f\Bigg|_{Y}.\] This map is surjective because every element of \(A(Y)\) is restriction of an element of \(k[x,y]=A(\mathbb A^k)\). Hence this map is a quotient map as this map is also a \(k-\)algebra map. If \(f\) and \(g\) are two elements of \(k(x,y)\), that restrict to the same function on \(Y\), then \(f-g\) must be identically zero on \(Y\). So \(f-g\in I(Y)\). The converse also holds, so the kernel of this map is exactly \(I(Y)\). So \(A(Y)=k[x,y]/I(Y)\). Note when we are thinking of \(A[Y]\) as the quotient ring, there is a concrete realization of it as a ring of functions on \(Y\), behind the algebraic object, such that any two polynomials in the equivalence classes given by the quotient map evaluate to the the same value when restricted to \(Y\).
When we say \(Y\) is the plane curve, we mean \(Y\) is the set of point satisfying the equation \(y=x^2\). The equation \(y=x^2\equiv y-x^2=0\). So a solution of this equation is same as the zero of the polynomial \(y-x^2\). So bringing everything to one side of the equation involving polynomials, the solution set becomes the zero set of a polynomials. So studying solutions of polynomial equations is equal to studying zeroes of polynomials. If \(I=(f)\), then \(Z(I)=Z(\{f\})=Z(f)\).
So \(Z((f))=Y\). \(A(Y) = k[x,y]/I(Z((f)))\).
By Hilbert’s Nullstellensatz \(I(Z((f))) = \sqrt {(f)}\). This is an important step.

Let \(f(x)=a_0x^n+a_1x^{n-1}+\cdots+a_n\) be a plynomial in \(\mathbb Z[x]\). Suppose there exists a prime number \(p\in\mathbb Z\) such that \(p\nmid a_0\), \(p|a_k\) for \(k>0\), and \(p^2\nmid a_n\). Then \(f(x)\) is irreducible in \(\mathbb Z[x]\).

Fact: For a ring \(R\), if \(\mathfrak p\) is a prime ideal in \(R\), then \(\mathfrak pR[x]\) is a prime ideal in \(R[x]\).
Proof: Consider the ring extension \(R\subset R[x]\). Then \(\mathfrak p^e\) the extension of \(\mathfrak p\) in \(R[x]\) is \(\mathfrak pR[x]\). The set of all polynomials in \(R[x]\) whose coefficients belong to \(\mathfrak p\) is denoted \(\mathfrak p[x]\). This is an ideal. We also have that \(\mathfrak pR[x]=\mathfrak p[x]\). This fact essentially gives us the description of \(\mathfrak p^e\) as all those polynomials whose coeeficients are in \(\mathfrak p\). This is also true for a general ideal \(I\) of \(R\). \(I^e=I[x]\), where \(I[x]\) is described analogously. Note: In a general extension \(R\subset S\), the extension ideals maynot have a such a simple descris iption. Consider the s.e.s (short exact sequence) \[0\to I\to R\to \frac{R}{I}\to 0.\] This is a s.e.s of \(R-\)modules.
For every ring \(R\), there is a canonical \(\mathbb Z\) algebra structure on \(R\) given by the the “cannonical” map \[\mathbb Z\to R, \quad n\mapsto n\cdot 1_R.\] Using this every \(R-\)module is canonically a \(\mathbb Z\) module and every \(R-\)module map is a \(\mathbb Z-\)module map. Hence the above s.e.s is also a sequence of \(\mathbb Z\) modules and \(\mathbb Z-\)module morphisms.
